notes.b: Coordination is the process of linking stimuli with responses so the body works as a whole. Humans have two coordinating systems: the nervous system and the hormonal (endocrine) system.

notes.h: Differences between nervous and hormonal coordination
points: Nature of the message: nervous, electrical impulses along neurons, with chemical neurotransmitters at synapses; hormonal, chemical hormones.
Route: nervous, along neurons directly to particular cells; hormonal, in the blood to all parts of the body.
Speed: nervous, very fast, with impulses arriving in a fraction of a second; hormonal, slower, taking seconds to hours as hormones travel in the blood.
Duration: nervous, short-lived, ending when the impulses stop; hormonal, longer-lasting, because hormones stay in the blood until they are broken down, mainly in the liver.
Area affected: nervous, localised to the muscle or gland the neuron reaches; hormonal, widespread, reaching every target cell with receptors for the hormone, possibly in many organs.
Effectors: nervous, muscles and glands; hormonal, target cells in organs and tissues.
Typical uses: nervous, rapid responses such as reflexes and movement; hormonal, long-term processes such as growth, metabolism, puberty and the menstrual cycle, and steady control of blood glucose.
Both use chemical messengers that bind to specific receptors on target cells: neurotransmitters in the nervous system and hormones in the hormonal system.
Both carry information from receptors or control centres to effectors, and both take part in homeostasis through negative feedback.

notes.h: How the two systems work together
points: The hypothalamus links the two systems: it is part of the brain but controls the pituitary gland.
In danger, nerve impulses stimulate the adrenal glands to release adrenaline, so a fast nervous response is followed by a longer-lasting hormonal one.
Touching a hot plate: nervous, a reflex, under a second, affecting one arm.
Rising blood glucose: hormonal, insulin, taking minutes to hours, affecting cells throughout the body.

keyTerms.definition: Linking stimuli with responses so that the body's systems work together as a whole.
A chemical messenger released at a synapse that carries a nerve impulse across the gap.
The gap between two neurons, or between a neuron and an effector, across which neurotransmitters pass.
A chemical messenger carried in the blood that affects only the target cells with receptors for it.
A cell with receptors that bind a particular hormone or neurotransmitter, so it responds to that messenger.
A rapid, automatic nervous response to a stimulus.
A hormone released by the adrenal glands in danger, which prepares the body for action.

questions.prompt: Give three differences between nervous and hormonal coordination.
questions.model: Route: nervous coordination sends impulses along neurons directly to particular cells, whereas hormones travel in the blood to all parts of the body. Speed: nervous responses are very fast, with impulses arriving in a fraction of a second, whereas hormonal responses are slower and take seconds to hours. Area affected: nervous effects are localised to the muscle or gland that the neuron reaches, whereas hormones affect every target cell with receptors for them, possibly in many organs.

questions.prompt: Explain how the nervous and hormonal systems work together when a person is frightened.
questions.model: The hypothalamus links the two systems: it is part of the brain but controls the pituitary gland. In danger, nerve impulses stimulate the adrenal glands to release adrenaline. The nervous response is fast, and the adrenaline response that follows is longer-lasting.
